findings.passage: That reading strains to explain a man who builds a protector into his rule for heretics, puts himself on the protected side, and tells being reined in as something he had coming.
findings.problem: The repaired 6-versus-8 test rests on 'which way the cover runs' and the premise 'An Eight gives cover and asks for none.' In the sources the article already uses, the cover runs both ways in his own account, and the reader is shown one. (1) Lonsdale interview, 27:28 to 27:46: the rule answers Lonsdale's question about why bureaucracies keep trying to kill heretics. He begins 'that question you just asked is why I wrote the book. We have to remember that we need the heretics', so it is what he says institutions owe them, and Lonsdale takes it that way ('every company needs to do this for their most talented people ... your job as a leader is to keep them'). He does not say there that he needed protection. (2) Face the Nation, 18:04 to 18:21, in the same answer the article paraphrases as Army human resourcing: 'how do we identify who these exceptional people are? How do we protect them?' That is Sankar on the giving side. (3) Hudson transcript, Karp's reply at the same dinner: 'maybe I've saved Shyam and others many, many times—but Shyam saved me after COVID', followed by Sankar arriving in New Hampshire to tell him 'This isn't cutting it. You got to get back.' (4) a16z interview, 16:29 to 17:25: he credits the general 'who protected' John Boyd. The evidence record lists this reading as an alternative (C193: 'He may be speaking as a leader who gives protection, not as someone who needs it'; C194: 'a manager's advice to other managers'), but the prose leaves it out and instead uses the rule as the one element the dinner cannot explain. 'Puts himself on the protected side' is an inference from his calling himself a heretic forty seconds later, written as description. The type FAQ and the Type 8 FAQ ('Type 6 leads on one main ground') repeat it. What survives the check is narrower: he describes leaning on a guide ('confidant', 'guru'), tells his father and Karp as right, and tells being corrected as deserved.
findings.acceptance_test: The Type 8 section says in plain words that the rule was given as what institutions and leaders owe their heretics, and that he also describes giving cover himself (the CBS 'How do we protect them?' line, quoted or paraphrased), with Karp's 'Shyam saved me' set beside 'rabbi' and 'guru'. 'Puts himself on the protected side' is cut or marked as this page's inference. 'One thing on record is hard to fit to a loyal Eight' and the FAQ's 'Type 6 leads on one main ground' are scaled to what the sources carry, or the section returns to saying the observations lean Six and none settles it. Both FAQs match the body. C150, C193, C194, C198, C199, C200 and type_hypothesis.discriminator record the S12 and S04 passages. The body stays within 4,500 words.

enneagram.passage: An Eight gives cover and asks for none.
enneagram.reason: The test is serious in design: it rejects the rebel caricature for a loyal Eight, gives Types 1 and 3 real trials, fronts his own denial of fear and names falsifiers. Against the standard's anchor it falls short on both counts. No costly choice is shown that the Six motive explains better than pay, position or rank; the page says so ('None of these deferrals cost him anything', 'Loyalty and money point the same way', 'the record is empty'). And the discriminator the repair put in the lead does not hold as written: in the same sources he speaks as the one who gives cover, Karp says 'Shyam saved me', and the rule is addressed to those at the top. What survives is a narrower pattern of self-narration (a guide he calls his guru, authorities told as right, forecasts of failure), mostly from one dinner and two friendly interviews, with three types still live by the article's own account. That is a reasoned leaning, not an alternative beaten on a sourced discriminator.
